subject: Is slow warmup indicative of 'necessity' or potentially wasteful?

messages.author: cf47bbe63da1f3ae
messages.subject: Is slow warmup indicative of 'necessity' or potentially wasteful?
parts: I have some rough understanding of how the warmup procedure works, but it's not entirely clear to me whether the fact that it is 'slow' (roughly 10x slower than sampling, per iteration) is something that can be substantially improved by adjusting parameters (so far I have just set the initial step size to roughly that used by NUTS during sampling), or whether this slowness is inherent to the problems of a) sampling towards high mass regions, and b) estimating the metric. Is there anything useful one can take from one fit procedure to the next, when fitting similar models with a similar parameter space, to different data?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is slow warmup indicative of 'necessity' or potentially wasteful?
parts:
I'm afraid we don't yet have a way to specify the mass matrix
for a run, but that's coming soon. Then you will be able to warm
start everything.

You can look at the traceplot to see what's going on. Sometimes
you need a different step size for the tails than the high mass
volume and Stan needs to adjust during warmup.

In addition to having reasonable priors, it helps immensely if
all the parameters are roughly unit scaled on the unconstrained
scale. Stan transforms all constrained variables to be unconstrained
(see manual for transforms) and applies the Jacobian of the inverse
transforms automatically. So you have to reason through what's going
on in the unconstrained space to really understand how Stan samples.

The closer you can get that to being unit normal on the margins
with no correlations, the easier time Stan will have sampling with
Euclidean HMC.

- Bob
